name: PURSUE Release 1
agencies: Department of War | NASA | Department of State | FBI
overview: PURSUE Release 1 (Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters), published 2026-05-08, contains 158 documents from the Department of War, NASA, the Department of State and the FBI. The notes cover about fifty of them. They fall into two groups: historical files from 1944 to the 1990s, and recent military sensor material from 2013 to 2025 submitted to AARO. The historical files are the most useful starting points. The FBI's 1947 compilation in case file 62-HQ-83894, Serial 130 gathers Kenneth Arnold's account, witness interviews, and an Air Force analysis of 18 sightings. The Twining memorandum package shows the Army Air Forces concluding the phenomenon was real and creating Project Sign, and it also records a photograph dismissed as film defects. Other items include an FBI report on the 1964 Socorro landing and a 1955 Air Attaché report of a sighting from a train in the USSR. The Socorro case rests on one primary witness. The 1955 report rests on a brief dusk sighting without sensor data. Many other FBI items are sections of the same 62-HQ-83894 file. They are described by metadata only, and one, Serial 164, is a procedural memorandum repeated in about fifteen copies. Several files are secondhand or have prosaic explanations in the record. The WWII SHAEF 'foofighter' file leaves the matter open but offers Me.262 aircraft and flak rockets as likely explanations. A 1952 State Department memo summarizes General Samford calling the subject a 'complete enigma' while allowing for radar 'electronic fluke'. The 1948 USAFE package relays Swedish conclusions rather than direct US observation. A COMETA report, a private French study that reached the extraterrestrial hypothesis, arrived through NASA correspondence and is not an official finding. Three box compilations of incident summaries are metadata-only descriptions, so their content is unverified. The recent material is mostly CENTCOM and AARO records. These include mission reports, range fouler forms and short infrared or full-motion videos, all labeled unresolved or given no conclusion. Many show only an 'area of contrast.' Some come with conventional readings: a balloon-like object traveling with the wind at 31,000 feet, a possible reflection on water, apparent size growth explained by the platform closing distance, and a radar jamming event attributed to a Turkish X-band jammer. One Syria-area crew assessed an infrared flare as benign. Many pages are fully redacted. Among the more detailed accounts is a multi-agent Western US report of orbs and kite-shaped objects, which AARO calls among its most compelling but which has no sensor data. A redacted 2025 statement describes a helicopter pursuit of orbs but offers no analysis.

name: PURSUE Release 2
agencies: CIA | Department of Energy | Department of War | NASA | Office of the Director of National Intelligence
overview: PURSUE Release 2, published 2026-05-22, contains 64 documents from the CIA, the Department of Energy, the Department of War, NASA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. The notes cover a subset of these files. Most of those are short AARO descriptions of infrared sensor videos, mostly from the CENTCOM area of responsibility between 2018 and 2022. Other videos come from NORTHCOM, EUCOM, AFRICOM, the Yellow Sea, the East China Sea and the Southeastern United States. A smaller group of older and non-video records adds historical context. The most substantial first-hand account is the senior intelligence officer's narrative of a late-2025 helicopter mission over a western test range. It describes orange orbs seen through night-vision goggles, FLIR and the naked eye, with radar detections reported from the Joint Operations Center. It is anonymous, has no classification markings and offers no explanation. Two Department of Energy files concern nuclear sites. Enhanced Pantex imagery is only pages 5 and 6 of a six-page report, and most of the text is withheld under UCNI. The Sandia Base file covers 209 reported sightings from 1948 to 1950 and mentions Project Grudge, but it was summarized from metadata only, so its contents are unverified here. Among the AARO videos, the most discussed is likely the F-16C shootdown video over Lake Huron, dated 12 February 2023. The title is uploader-defined, the callsign and weapon are redacted, and AARO declines to judge what the footage shows. The Syrian 'instant acceleration' video was digitally altered before upload, and the apparent acceleration may simply reflect the sensor ceasing to track. Other files describe sensor-tracked 'areas of contrast,' including four objects in apparent formation and the Coast Guard C-144 'Tic Tac' clips from 2024. Readers should weigh these videos cautiously. AARO states that many lack a substantiated chain-of-custody, offers no analytical conclusion on any of them, and notes that several were digitally altered. Many contain long blank stretches, with only seconds of relevant content. Titles such as 'Spherical UAP' come from anonymous uploaders and are not endorsed by AARO. Two files, PR057a and PR057b, are duplicates of the same Yellow Sea video. The historical items are less dramatic. The Mercury-Atlas 7 account of Scott Carpenter's 'snowflake' particles has a conventional explanation in the record: ice crystals venting from the spacecraft. A 1973 CIA report from Sary Shagan mentions a green circular phenomenon only in a single paragraph of a broader report on a weapons range, and the source offered no opinion on it. The Department of Energy's 1970s Tuck letters are informal recollections, not incident reports.

name: PURSUE Release 3
agencies: CIA | Department of War | FBI | Intelligence Community Agency | NASA | U.S. Government
overview: PURSUE Release 3 contains 72 documents from the CIA, the Department of War, the FBI, an Intelligence Community Agency, NASA and the wider U.S. Government. The material falls into two main groups: Cold War-era administrative and intelligence records, and a large set of recent witness accounts, mostly from 2021 to 2026. Many files in the release are metadata-only entries, digital renderings or procedural papers rather than incident reports, so the number of documents overstates the amount of primary sighting evidence. The historical group is the most substantial. The CIA folder on the Robertson Panel of 1953 records the panel's finding of no direct threat to national security and its recommendation to reduce public interest in the subject. The Department of War holds a transmittal copy of that report. Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 is a statistical study of roughly 4,000 reports. It classed 19.7% of 2,199 object sightings as unknown, yet concluded that it was highly improbable any of them involved technology beyond current science. A 1949 Army evaluation found only about 20% of some 210 incidents explained, but it saw no evidence of foreign involvement and expected most of the rest to prove natural or domestic in origin. Other items from this period are procedural, such as the 1948 Navy reporting directive, a CIA status memo on Project Bluebook, and a 1958 memo on handling a civilian researcher. They carry little sighting data. The CIA's foreign-source reports are mostly unevaluated and second-hand. The 1968 report from Ladakh, Nepal, Sikkim and Bhutan describes a metallic disc found in a crater, but the source is redacted and the report is marked not finally evaluated. The Baku, Budapest and Sary Shagan items rest on single witnesses or relayed letters, and the record itself suggests Soviet testing as a plausible context for some. The 2008 Harare report is unresolved and mentions possible radar corroboration only tentatively. The recent material centers on two clusters. The first is the October 2023 western United States event, where six federal agents described orbs apparently launching smaller orbs. In its AARO update, AARO attributes about 60% of the activity to military aircraft dispensing flares and leaves about 40% unresolved. That 40% rests on testimony alone, and the five narrative statements, the notional map and the FBI renderings add no sensor data. The second cluster is a series of FBI reports from the northeastern United States, including agents' own observations in November 2024 and civilian iPhone videos. The Colorado Springs case has an intelligence community analysis that offers a low-confidence conventional explanation, backscattered sunlight, while the case stays unresolved. A December 2024 FBI site survey found nothing unusual, and the NASA items are brief or metadata-only.

name: PURSUE Release 4
agencies: CIA | Department of Energy | Department of War | FBI | NASA
overview: PURSUE Release 4, published 2026-07-10, contains 40 documents from the CIA, the Department of Energy, the Department of War, the FBI and NASA. Roughly half are short infrared sensor videos submitted to AARO. The rest are historical studies and correspondence from the late 1940s through the 1970s, a small group of Space Shuttle photographs, and several files that have little or no connection to unidentified aerial phenomena. The historical material is the most substantive. The Air Force and Naval Intelligence study of about 210 incidents, available as Air Intelligence Division Study No. 203 and in a 1949-dated copy, concludes that some type of flying object has been observed but cannot be identified, and it treats Soviet origin as a possibility. It is a provisional analysis with considerable speculation. The Department of Energy file Los Alamos Conference on Aerial Phenomena is a transcript of a 1949 meeting on green fireballs near New Mexico atomic installations. The meteor expert said the events were not conventional meteor falls, but no consensus was reached and all observations were visual. The CIA's memorandum on the 1955 train sighting records four witnesses whose accounts differed, and it concludes that steep-climbing aircraft or missiles were the probable explanation. A companion CIA memo from the same year finds one witness's testimony insufficient to confirm any unconventional aircraft. Two further Department of War files concern policy rather than incidents. The committee review of Project Blue Book covers the university study that led to the Condon Report and includes the Robertson Panel report. Its meeting notes describe the UFO problem as '99% public relations.' The 1955 Blue Book correspondence and the joint U.S.-Canadian aviation file were summarized from metadata only, so their contents are unverified. The most recent substantive case is the Pantex incident report, which describes an object tracked by radar and seen by security personnel over a nuclear weapons facility in 2015. It remains under investigation with no stated conclusion, though its slow speed and small size are consistent with a drone or balloon. Much of the release is of limited evidential value. The AARO videos, from the South China Sea, Yellow Sea, East China Sea, Middle East, Atlantic and United States, are all listed as unresolved. Most show only an 'area of contrast' lasting seconds, from a single sensor. Several were digitally altered before submission, and one carries an AARO technical comment attributing its flicker to auto-gain control. The Atlantic 2020 case resembles a deformed balloon drifting with the wind. The three STS-80 photographs show a small object that may be debris or a window artifact. The four Apollo debriefings concern cosmic-ray light flashes, a known biological effect, and the FBI file records a child's report and a statement that the Bureau collects no UFO information.

name: PURSUE Release 5
agencies: CIA | Department of State | Department of War | Executive Office of the President | FBI
overview: PURSUE Release 5 contains 41 documents from the CIA, the Department of State, the Department of War, the Executive Office of the President and the FBI. The set splits into two groups: a small number of historical records from 1947 to 1965, and a larger group of recent material from 2019 to 2026, made up mostly of video clips and FBI interview reports with their illustrations. The historical records are the most substantive. The CIA file on a 1964 radar and visual encounter near Puerto Rico has a CIA analysis concluding the object was probably a delta-wing fighter of unknown origin. Both domestic experimental aircraft and simple misidentification were considered and ruled out. The CIA also notes the radar was in an evaluation program at the time and that the foreign-fighter hypothesis lacks supporting evidence. The companion briefing notes for Walter Elder leave the case unresolved. A 1947 War Department review of Scandinavian ghost rocket reports attributes most sightings to meteors or other mundane causes, and finds that no physical fragments were recovered. A summary of Air Materiel Command's Project Sign work records no conclusive proof of real aircraft, and the analysis behind it is based only on the file's description. The 1953 Navy film analysis is also described from metadata only. The 1963 Brazil material is routine by comparison. A State Department airgram calls the reported Bahia crash apparently fabricated and notes a flat denial from the Brazilian Ministry of Aeronautics. A companion cable records a weather balloon as the tentative identification and no object found on the ground. The related White House space council file is only a relayed radio report. The Department of War entries are mostly short infrared clips. Seven of them show an AC-130J sensor display over the Gulf of Oman in 2021 and are secondary phone recordings of a screen. The associated intelligence report on that AC-130 encounter describes roughly 25 cold orbs but is explicitly unevaluated, and its primary video was lost to a recorder failure. A further group of 2019 Pacific clips was digitally altered before reaching AARO, and the Middle East clips from 2023 and 2025 show only an unspecified area of contrast. These descriptions offer no range, size or speed, and mundane causes are not excluded. The FBI portion is mostly witness testimony from heavily redacted FD-302 reports, such as the Bagram triangle and airborne lights interview. Several accounts have no sensor corroboration, and one event was reported 14 years after it occurred. The rest of the FBI material is digital renderings produced in 2026 from witness descriptions. They are illustrations, not evidence, and at least two do not match the titles of the reports they accompany.

name: PURSUE Release 6
agencies: Department of War | Local Law Enforcement
overview: PURSUE Release 6 contains 75 documents, almost all from the Department of War, plus a small set from local law enforcement in Colorado. The notes cover roughly 50 of them. They fall into four groups: 1952 Air Force records, recent CENTCOM and Indo-Pacific Command sensor reports, Colorado police videos, and a large block of administrative and technical papers from the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP). The historical material is the most informative. The transcript of Captain Edward J. Ruppelt's March 1952 briefing reviews about 800 Air Force case files, of which roughly 20% from credible observers were unexplained. It records reports clustering near nuclear and security sites and calls for systematic data collection, while acknowledging that no physical proof was held. A matching audio file also covers the briefing. A second cluster concerns the July 1952 Tremonton, Utah film. The Project Blue Book photo file on the Tremonton film discusses pillow balloons and birds, and later Air Force assessments favored seabirds reflecting sunlight, so the case was never fully closed but has a conventional leading explanation. The film copy itself appears to be a composite with unrelated sewing footage, and the Navy personnel record for the photographer adds background only. The modern reports come mainly from CENTCOM and INDOPACOM, submitted to AARO. Three mission reports stand out: a 2022 Iraq mission report of objects 1-2 meters in size moving at 80-180 mph, a July 2025 report of six small spherical objects, and an October 2025 report of a white orb. Each is listed as unresolved, but the notes show single-observer estimates, no radar corroboration, redactions, and in the 2022 report a label of 'UAS' and dust-degraded sensors. The paired infrared videos and stills, including several short Yellow Sea and East China Sea clips, describe only an 'area of contrast' with no range or size data. Two Iraq stills show a trail the description attributes to compression artifacts. The Colorado law enforcement items are cellphone videos and transcripts from 2023 and 2024 describing lights with red, blue and green flashing. AARO notes that autofocus and processing can distort apparent shape and motion. One transcript contains only three brief utterances and no description of an object, and another relies on an officer's verbal claim of a radar check with no data. The largest block by count is AAWSAP: contract documents and modifications involving Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, and about two dozen Defense Intelligence Reference Documents on propulsion, materials, and physics. The AAWSAP Statement of Objectives is the best starting point for the program. These files are administrative or theoretical, contain no incident data, and mostly were assessed from metadata only. The injury-focused paper, the DIRD on field effects on human tissue, is also a literature synthesis that establishes no causal link.

name: PURSUE Release 7
agencies: Department of War | FBI | Executive Office of the President | U.S. Government
overview: PURSUE Release 7 contains 28 documents from the Department of War, the FBI, the Executive Office of the President and the wider U.S. Government. Most of the material is historical or contractor-produced. Only two files describe recent incidents: both concern a June 2026 sighting of a small, dark triangular object by federal agents at a site in the western United States. The AARO account, the AARO memorandum for record, records a witness debrief and no conclusive finding. The FBI's FD-302 statement covers what appears to be the same event. Both rest on witness accounts alone. The FBI file's photographs seem to show only a marker overlaid on a static landscape, so they are not independent sensor evidence, and names, dates and locations are heavily redacted. The largest group is made up of Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) papers from 2008 to 2010, produced under the DIA-administered AAWSAP. They include monthly reports for March, April, June and November 2009, a December 2008 project plan, the Project CAPELLA proposal, MUFON white papers, and a Utah ranch investigation. Two are worth opening for different reasons. The BAASS self-assessment excerpts a DIA assessment of the 2004 Nimitz 'Tic Tac' encounter, though its speed and acceleration figures rest on assumed inputs. The Utah ranch report is notable because its DNA analysis identified hair samples as raccoon and domestic dog. Elsewhere in this group the files are administrative, speculative or built on unverified civilian testimony. One includes cases with Chinese lanterns suggested as an explanation. The November 2009 report was summarized from its description only. A second group is Air Force intelligence reports from 1949 to 1957, drawn from Saudi Arabia, Guam, Canada, Sweden, Italy, Morocco, Germany, Alaska, Indiana and Catalina Island. Most are single-witness or radar-only accounts with no corroboration, and many carry no evaluation. Several have conventional answers in the record. The Morocco radar report attributes the returns to anomalous propagation, ship radar jamming or birds. A Catalina Island file concludes the object was Jupiter, and another assessed a sighting as a probable meteor. The Guam report allows that a malfunctioning weather balloon could explain the sighting. The Saudi Arabia B-52 report is unredacted but offers only a brief radar-only contact and no conclusion. The remainder is background material rather than sighting reports. Two files on 1962 to 1964 space-debris recovery policy contain no UAP observation, and the Air Force personnel record of a Project SIGN and GRUDGE-era intelligence officer was summarized from metadata only. Readers looking for incident descriptions can skip these.
